chap2-mission1-scene1.explanation: Listening to both families helps the leader learn what the disagreement is about. Look at what the leader does, rather than only remembering the leader's title. The story shows one situation; it does not mean every community made decisions in the same way.
chap2-mission1-scene1.example: Made-up classroom example: two groups want to use the same reading corner. Ask each group what it needs before suggesting a plan. In the lesson, notice how hearing both families helps the leader understand their concerns.
chap2-mission1-scene1.guidingQuestion: What important information might the leader miss by hearing only one family?

vocabulary.definition: A worry, need or problem that someone wants to explain.

chap2-mission1-scene4.explanation: A custom is a practice people learn from others. It is not always a written law. To understand the disagreement in this story, find out which practice this community follows. Do not assume that every community follows the same one.
chap2-mission1-scene4.example: Made-up classroom example: one class uses a talking card to take turns speaking. Another class raises hands. Ask how each class takes turns before deciding which practice applies there. This comparison helps explain why the explorer asks about the local custom in the story.
chap2-mission1-scene4.guidingQuestion: Why should the explorer ask about this community's custom instead of assuming it is the same everywhere?

vocabulary.definition: A practice people learn and pass on in a group or community.

chap2-mission2-scene2.explanation: The child in the story explains why a place matters to their community. Say whose belief you are describing and who shared it. The lesson explains that communities could have different beliefs; one person's explanation does not tell us what everyone believed.
chap2-mission2-scene2.example: Made-up reading example: a story character says a stream is special to their family. Ask what the stream means to that character and who shared the story. Do not assume that every family would explain it in the same way.
chap2-mission2-scene2.guidingQuestion: How could you describe the child's explanation without saying that everyone shared the same belief?

vocabulary.definition: The person, record or object from which information comes.

chap2-mission2-scene3.explanation: A ritual has actions that carry meaning for the people taking part. In this story, a community member explains that the gathering gives thanks for the harvest. Look for that explanation of its purpose. Food or a gathering alone does not tell us what every ritual meant.
chap2-mission2-scene3.example: Made-up story example: families prepare food for a thanksgiving gathering after a harvest. An explorer asks, 'What does this gathering mean to you?' Their answer helps explain its purpose. Another gathering could have a different purpose.
chap2-mission2-scene3.guidingQuestion: Which clue explains why the families are taking part, rather than only what they are doing?
